1.pericope_label: Afterward he brought me again unto the door of the house; and, behold, waters issued out from under the threshold of the house eastward
debates: Whether the waters are literal or ideal
Why the stream is deflected southward at the start
outliers: Henry argues that the waters cannot be the pipes that washed the sacrifices, since that would turn a pleasant river into a common sewer, and infers a spiritual meaning for the rest of the vision
Clarke states flatly that no such waters were ever in the temple and that a fountain of such abundance could not be on the top of such a hill
Wesley alone reads the passage as plumbing, a fountain to the west and conduit pipes bringing water under the east gate
Ellicott holds the whole is ideal, the river swelling without any tributary in direct opposition to the ordinary course of nature
themes: A pleasant river turned into a common sewer
Grace said to come drop by drop and be given as it can be used
A river impassable within a mile and a half of its source
A truth made known by degrees to one who had walked past it repeatedly

6.pericope_label: And it shall come to pass, that every thing that liveth, which moveth, whithersoever the rivers shall come, shall live
debates: Whether the dual form means two rivers or one
Where the second fountain named lay
Why the marshes are left unhealed
outliers: Ellicott holds only one river is meant and offers three accounts of the dual form, an allusion to the Jordan, an expression of greatness, or a redivision of the word giving river of the sea
Ellicott prefers to place the second fountain on the eastern side of the sea, so that the phrase means its whole breadth, against an older writer who set it at the mouth of the Jordan
Ellicott takes the unhealed marshes to show that the effect of the waters ceases where the waters cease, and that a perfect and universal obedience is not to be expected as the effect of the gospel
Ellicott answers the objection that nothing can be made of the fishermen by noting that a figure must contain details with nothing answering to them in the thing signified
themes: A prophet told to walk along a bank he had never left
Salt crust left bare as a flood subsides
Fishermen who would have no place at all on a literal reading
A river that displaces the Jordan without mentioning it

13.pericope_label: And ye shall inherit it, one as well as another: concerning the which I lifted up mine hand to give it unto your fathers: and this land shall fall unto you for inheritance
debates: What the equality of the portions consists in
outliers: Gill argues from the size, the border being larger than the land under Moses or Joshua or after the captivity, that either a converted Israel or the church is meant
Ellicott takes the equality to be of the width of the strips, and observes that this makes the actual areas very unequal, the land being nearly three times as broad at the south as at the north
Ellicott traces out what the map would look like were the portions made actually equal, moving the oblation south and setting the temple near Hebron
Ellicott notes the Hebrew says only Joseph portions in the plural, since that they should be two and no more needed no specifying
themes: A promise long contradicted by providence and kept at last
A map redrawn on a suggestion never adopted
Boundaries fixed to keep neighbours out and the people in
An earlier survey that began where this one ends

15.pericope_label: And it shall come to pass, that ye shall divide it by lot for an inheritance unto you, and to the strangers that sojourn among you
debates: Which Tamar is meant on the southern border
Whether the tribes east of the Jordan are provided for
outliers: Ellicott holds the starting point on the Mediterranean cannot be determined, since it is unclear whether the tribal lines ran perpendicular to the Jordan or to the sea
Ellicott observes that the eastern boundary is the Jordan in both surveys, so that the two and a half tribes who had always lived east of it receive portions on the west
Gill rejects the identification of Tamar with Jericho given by three authorities and with a northern city given by a fourth, preferring a place by the Dead Sea
Clarke holds the division can have no reference but to the gospel, since no such division ever literally took place
themes: Portions west of the river for tribes who had always lived east of it
A place located only by reference to another place
Children invested with a right of inheriting from their birth
A defile whose entrance the authorities cannot agree on
